prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. The case for dropping it is not foolish, and it deserves a fair hearing before it is answered. Children now grow up surrounded by screens. Adults rarely write anything longer than a shopping list by hand, and the keyboard, the touchscreen and the voice assistant have taken over most of the work that handwriting once did. Cursive, the argument goes, is a Victorian accomplishment kept alive by nostalgia and by the sort of teacher who likes a neat page. Classroom hours are scarce, and every week spent looping letters together is a week not spent on coding, reasoning or reading. Several American states dropped cursive from their standards in the early 2010s, and some have since restored it. Finland removed it as a compulsory subject in 2016. If the skill is dying, why prop it up?

The answer begins with what handwriting is for. Most people assume its purpose is the production of text, and on that narrow view the keyboard wins easily. But in a primary school, handwriting is not mainly a way of getting words onto a page. It is a way of training a child's hand, eye and mind to work together, and it is a tool that shapes how children think while they write. The research here is not perfect, and I do not want to overstate it, but it points in a consistent direction. Studies using brain imaging have found that children who form letters by hand show richer activity in the regions linked to reading and language than children who type or trace the same letters. Experiments comparing note-taking by hand and by laptop have often found that handwriting produces better conceptual understanding, partly because the slowness forces the writer to compress and select rather than transcribe. Even if one treats individual findings with caution, the overall picture is that the motor effort of forming a letter helps the letter stick. A child who has written an a, a b and a c a few hundred times knows them differently from a child who has pressed the same keys.

That is an argument for handwriting in general, and a sceptic will quickly say that print handwriting would do just as well. Why join the letters at all? Here the case for cursive in particular has to be made on its own terms, and it rests on fluency. Joined writing is, when it is taught properly, faster than printing, because the pen stays on the paper and the hand moves in a continuous rhythm instead of lifting after every letter. Each lift is a small interruption, and a child who is still thinking about how to form a letter has less attention left for what the sentence is meant to say. Speed matters more than it sounds. A child who writes slowly and effortfully tends to write less, to choose simpler words because they are easier to spell and shape, and to lose the thread of an idea before it reaches the page. Teachers see this every year with children who have a great deal to say and cannot get it down. Fluent handwriting is not a luxury for such a child. It is the difference between expressing a thought and abandoning it.

There is also a pattern worth noticing in how children's handwriting actually develops. Many children who are taught only to print eventually invent their own joins in secondary school, because printing at speed is awkward and the hand wants to run letters together. The result is often an unplanned, idiosyncratic scrawl, a half-joined hybrid that nobody taught and nobody corrected. This is the real alternative to teaching cursive well. It is not a generation of confident printers; it is a generation that picks up a messy, improvised joined style under exam pressure, with no foundation in letter formation. Teaching a clear joined script in the primary years gives children a model that is legible and efficient, and it means the habits they carry into adolescence were chosen on purpose.

Cursive may also help some children who struggle most. The evidence is thinner here and I will not pretend otherwise, but a number of specialists working with dyslexic and dyspraxic children have long recommended joined writing, for reasons that make intuitive sense. Because each word is formed in one continuous movement, children are less likely to reverse letters, such as b and d, whose printed forms mirror each other. Because the spaces fall between words rather than between letters, the shape of a word becomes a single motor pattern, which can support spelling by building a kind of muscle memory for common letter strings. Not every child benefits, and some find joining harder than printing. A sensible school should allow for that. But the fact that the method helps some of the children who find literacy hardest is a reason to keep it available, not to remove it for everyone.

Now consider the objection that time is short. It is true, and it should be taken seriously, but the numbers rarely support the complaint. Handwriting practice in a good primary school takes perhaps fifteen minutes a few times a week, and it is often woven into spelling and composition rather than sitting apart from them. Against that modest cost, we have to set what children also lose if the skill disappears: the ability to read the handwriting of others. A child who has never seen or written cursive cannot read a grandparent's birthday card, a historical document, a teacher's comment in the margin or an old family letter. This sounds like a small thing until one imagines a whole generation cut off from the handwritten record of its own culture. Archives, wills, diaries and the notes of its own relatives will all be written in a script it cannot decipher without translation. We do not usually regard literacy as complete when a person can read only print produced after a certain date.

The sceptic's best reply is that none of this is decisive. Keyboard skills are also vital, and typing is a form of literacy children will use every day of their working lives. That is perfectly true, and nobody serious proposes that schools should abandon it. The choice, however, is a false one. Children can and should learn to type and to write by hand, just as they can learn to read from screens and from books. Teaching one skill does not require neglecting the other, and the strongest schools manage both. The danger is not that typing is taught but that handwriting is quietly allowed to lapse because it is no longer examined, no longer fashionable and no longer valued by adults who have stopped doing it themselves. Skills that are not taught rarely survive, and once the knowledge has gone out of the teaching profession it is expensive to recover. Countries that scrapped handwriting instruction have in some cases found themselves reversing course after teachers reported that children could not write legibly or at speed in examinations that still required it.

That last point deserves emphasis, because it brings the argument back to practice. Written examinations still exist, and for the foreseeable future they will. A child who cannot write legibly and quickly by hand will be disadvantaged in them, however brilliant at the keyboard. Marks are lost when an examiner cannot read an answer, and ideas are lost when the hand falls behind the mind. Fluent joined writing is one of the least glamorous but most reliable advantages a school can give a child, and it costs very little. It is also a matter of fairness, since the children who miss out are not those with computers and tutors at home but those who rely on school to teach them everything.

None of this means that handwriting should be taught as it was a century ago, with rigid slants, punishments for ink blots and a single approved style. The goal is not copperplate. It is a clear, fluent, legible hand that a child can produce without thinking, so that thought is free for other things. A modern approach might begin with simple letter forms that lend themselves to joining, introduce joins gradually once formation is secure, and allow children to settle into a personal style within a legible framework. It might pay attention to posture, grip and pace, and it should treat difficulties as something to support rather than shame. That is a reform worth having, and it is a far cry from abolition.

In the end the question is what we think primary school is for. If its only purpose were to prepare children for the immediate demands of the workplace, one might argue about whether a pen has any future in it. But primary education also builds the underlying capacities, the patience, the coordination, the sense of language as something made by the body as well as the mind, on which everything later depends. Joined-up handwriting is a small part of that work, but it is a real one. It helps children think, helps many of them spell and read, gives them a fast and legible way of getting ideas onto paper, and keeps them connected to the written past. We should not give it up merely because we no longer notice how much it quietly does for us.
